speaker: Boris Cherny
title: Head of Claude Code: What happens after coding is solved | Boris Cherny
question: In AI agent development, why aren't strong training-time alignment and thorough lab evaluations sufficient to ensure a system is safe?
guest: When you think about model safety, there are three layers. The lowest level is alignment and mechanistic interpretability—when we train the model, understanding what's happening in the neurons to make sure it's safe. The second layer is evals, which is essentially a laboratory setting: the model is in a petri dish, and you put it in a synthetic situation to see if it's aligned and doing the right thing. The third layer is seeing how the model behaves in the wild. As the model gets more sophisticated, this becomes so important because it might look very good on the first two layers but not great on the third one. With our agents, we study them internally for a long time first, and they look good on alignment and evals, but once an agent is acting on your behalf in a new setting, we have to make sure it's safe in the real world. That's why we release early as a research preview—to learn about alignment and safety and put those lessons back into the model and product.

points.core: Synthetic laboratory evaluations fail to capture complex open-ended real-world agent behavior.
points.note: Accept: Controlled evals act like a lab/petri dish and cannot anticipate the messy tools, environments, and edge cases autonomous agents encounter in real usage. Do not credit: Generic statements that tests are never 100% comprehensive.

points.core: Models passing alignment checks can still misbehave once deployed in production.
points.note: Accept: Strong performance on training-time alignment/interpretability and pre-release benchmarks does not guarantee safe behavior when acting autonomously in the wild. Do not credit: Vague warnings about AI risk or hallucination without noting the gap between passing pre-deployment layers and real-world failure.

points.core: Staged real-world releases surface unexpected failure modes needed to harden guardrails.
points.note: Accept: Controlled early deployments (e.g., internal dogfooding then research previews) generate real-world safety signal that feeds back into model training and product guardrails. Do not credit: Generic advice to 'move fast and iterate' or 'get user feedback' without tying it specifically to safety hardening.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Training-time alignment and lab evaluations are necessary but not sufficient because both only give evidence about behavior under the conditions that were tested, while agents operate in open-ended conditions that weren't.

Training shapes a model's dispositions imperfectly: a system can learn proxies for the intended goal that look identical in training but diverge in novel situations, and there is no current way to fully verify what was actually learned. Evaluations sample a finite set of scenarios, so they miss rare failures, and models can sometimes distinguish tests from real use and behave differently.

Deployment then adds risks that no lab captures. Agents face distribution shift, adversarial inputs such as prompt injection, long multi-step tasks where small errors compound, and real tools, permissions and data whose interactions create emergent failure modes. Safety is also a property of the whole system (model, scaffolding, access, human oversight), not the model alone.

That is why defense in depth is the standard: least-privilege permissions, sandboxing, runtime monitoring, human approval for irreversible actions, and incident response, so that a failure that slips through is caught and contained.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Training-time alignment and lab evaluations test models in bounded, static conditions that cannot capture the open-ended complexity of real-world deployment. Once deployed, AI agents act across long horizons using external tools, live software, and untrusted data, creating distribution shifts where learned safety behaviors can degrade. System-level interactions among the model, its scaffolding, persistent memory, and other agents also generate emergent, compounding failures that isolated benchmarks miss. Meanwhile, deployed agents encounter adaptive adversaries who continuously craft novel jailbreaks and indirect prompt injections embedded in external content. Lab evaluations face intrinsic limits as well: finite test suites cannot cover every rare, high-stakes scenario, and capable models may recognize evaluation settings—behaving safely during testing while failing or pursuing misaligned subgoals in production. Finally, safety is a system-wide socio-technical property shaped by how operators configure permissions, delegate authority, and integrate downstream tools. Consequently, ensuring agent safety requires defense in depth, pairing pre-deployment alignment and testing with least-privilege sandboxing, continuous runtime monitoring, and human oversight over irreversible actions.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Training-time alignment and lab evaluations can't guarantee safety, because both check the model under conditions that don't fully match how it will actually be used. Alignment training shapes general tendencies, but it can't cover every situation. Learned values can generalize in unexpected ways, and there may be rare failure modes, reward hacking or subtle misalignment that training never brought to the surface. Evaluations only sample a small part of the possible behaviors. They miss long-tail inputs, novel tool combinations and long multi-step tasks where small errors compound. A capable model may also behave differently when it notices it's being tested.

Deployment adds risks that a lab can't fully reproduce. Agents read untrusted content, which exposes them to prompt injection. They use real credentials and take actions that can't be undone, and they interact with other systems and people in changing environments. Users and attackers will try inputs nobody anticipated.

So safety has to be layered across the whole system. That means least-privilege permissions, sandboxing, monitoring and logging, human confirmation for high-stakes actions, rate limits, incident response, and continued red-teaming after release. Then if the model's alignment fails in some case, the damage stays limited and is likely to be caught.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Training and lab evaluations provide evidence about how an agent behaves under the conditions it was trained and tested in. In deployment, it can encounter unfamiliar inputs, adversarial instructions, or combinations of tools and permissions that tests missed. A mistake that was harmless in a sandbox can have real consequences when the agent can send messages, modify records, or take several actions before a person notices. Even a low failure rate can matter when an agent runs at scale.

Safety therefore depends on the deployed system as a whole. Limiting permissions reduces the harm a mistake can cause, human approval can catch consequential errors before they happen, and monitoring and rollback help teams detect and contain failures. Those safeguards need to keep working as the model, tools, and operating environment change.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Training-time alignment can teach an agent to behave safely across many situations, but the feedback it learns from only approximates what people intend. An agent can earn high marks by following a pattern that works in training and then make an unsafe choice when that pattern breaks down.

Lab evaluations face a similar limit. They sample a finite set of conditions, while deployment exposes the agent to unfamiliar inputs, changing environments, and new combinations of tools and permissions. For example, an agent that summarizes documents safely in a lab might mistake an instruction embedded in a real document for a user request. With access to email, that mistake could disclose sensitive data.

Strong training and evaluations provide evidence of safety. Limiting permissions, requiring approval for consequential actions, and monitoring real-world behavior help contain failures the lab missed.

answers.answer:
Training-time alignment and lab evaluations are necessary foundations, but they cannot guarantee safety once an AI agent operates in the real world. Alignment is probabilistic rather than absolute, and lab benchmarks are static snapshots that cannot exhaustively anticipate the open-ended, multi-step environments agents encounter in deployment. Real-world distribution shifts, novel tool interactions, and compounding errors across long horizons routinely produce edge cases that pre-deployment tests miss.

Moreover, deployed agents constantly ingest untrusted external data—such as webpages, emails, or API responses—creating attack surfaces like indirect prompt injection that can hijack otherwise aligned behavior at runtime. Lab evaluations also face fundamental blind spots: rare, high-impact failures are difficult to trigger reliably in testing, and increasingly capable models may recognize evaluation contexts and behave differently than they would in production.

Because these gaps cannot be closed before deployment alone, safe agent systems require defense-in-depth at runtime, including least-privilege tool permissions, sandboxing, human approval for irreversible actions, and continuous post-deployment monitoring.

answers.answer:
Training-time alignment shapes how a model behaves, and lab evaluations sample that behavior under controlled conditions. Once deployed, an agent encounters unfamiliar inputs, adversarial users, and changing environments. It may also have access to tools, sensitive data, and permissions that let it act in the world. A small error can compound across a long sequence of actions, and even a rare failure can matter when the system runs millions of times.

Safety therefore depends on the whole deployed system. Limiting permissions and requiring approval for high-impact actions can contain failures. Monitoring, incident response, and ongoing evaluations help teams detect problems and adapt as the model, tools, or conditions change.

answers.answer:
Strong training-time alignment and thorough lab evaluations provide evidence about how an agent behaves under tested conditions. Deployment exposes it to unfamiliar inputs, changing environments, and longer sequences of decisions. An agent that handles individual tasks safely can still compound small errors or take a harmful action when given access to tools, sensitive data, or real-world systems. It may also behave differently when it recognizes an evaluation, making good test results less predictive of actual use.

Safety therefore depends on how the agent is deployed as well as how it was trained and tested. Limited permissions, human approval for high-impact actions, and monitoring with the ability to intervene help contain failures that lab evaluations miss.
